item: Layout D1
detail: Word bulletins: "Prison Population & Accommodation Briefing". Total = male + female + prisoners held in police/court cells under Operation Safeguard. No IRC split.

item: Layout D2
detail: Word bulletins switch to "Population and Capacity Briefing". Total includes NOMS-operated IRCs.

item: Layout A1
detail: XLS/ODS, columns Total | Prisons | NOMS (later HMPPS) Operated IRCs. Total INCLUDES IRCs.

item: IRC naming
detail: "NOMS Operated IRCs" becomes "HMPPS Operated IRCs". Same series.

item: Layout A2
detail: Single "This week" column. IRC breakdown dropped; rows renamed to "Population in male/female estate".

item: Operating Margin row appears
detail: Margin first published as an explicit row in the weekly bulletin.

item: Layout B + reporting day change
detail: New "Data" sheet, columns Total | Adult Male | Female | YCS. Headroom published directly. Reporting day moves Friday to Monday. YCS separated out.

item: Operating margin 2,000
detail: Stated in definitions text as "less 2,000 places".

item: Margin stepped down
detail: 2,250 to 2,000 to 1,950 to 1,830 to 1,680 to 1,480 to 1,340 across 2022-23, per the 12-months-ago column.

item: Margin 1,350
detail: Settles at 1,350 for the adult male + female + YCS estate combined.

item: Margin 1,640
detail: Raised from 1,350 to 1,640 (adult male 1,460, female 120, YCS 60). Raises published headroom by 290 with no change in physical capacity.

item: Source date error
detail: MoJ dates this bulletin Saturday 5 Nov 2011. Every other 2011 bulletin is a Friday. Reference date is almost certainly Fri 4 Nov. Left as published and flagged.
evidence: title and in-file date both say 05/11/2011

item: Stale in-file dates
detail: In-file cell date disagrees with the title date by 5 to 365 days; title date used because it falls on the era reporting weekday.

item: Capacity restatement
detail: Bulletin reports last-week UOC as 80,904 where the previous bulletin published 80,912. 8-place restatement, unexplained.
evidence: weekly_consistency_report.csv, the only mismatch in 711 pairs

item: Skipped weeks
detail: 24 gaps of 14 days and 3 of 21 days, clustered on Easter and New Year. One recovered from the following bulletin last-week block; the rest have no published value.

item: Projection layout: scenario columns
detail: Central path is labelled Medium, No change, Scenario 2 or Central depending on edition. Scenario 2 is CENTRAL in the 2012 and 2013 editions but HIGH in the 2014 edition, so generic scenario labels must be resolved against the explicit central column.

item: Projection layout: single central path
detail: Table A1/1.1 switches from scenario columns to one central path broken down by sentence type (Remand, Determinate, Indeterminate, Recall, Non-Criminal, Fine Defaulters). Low/high move to a separate uncertainty table.

item: Projection reference month moves
detail: End June for 2008-2019 editions, 1 June in 2017-2022, end September in 2020-2026, 1 July in 2021-2026, end November in 2022-2027 and 2023-2028, end September from 2024-2029. Horizons are not comparable without using the published dates.

item: Short central table
detail: Table A1 publishes only four forward years (2017 to 2020), not five.

item: Central block truncated in source
detail: Table 1.1 Central block stops at November 2024 while the Low and High blocks run to November 2026. The missing central years are recoverable from the Table A4 monthly appendix.

item: Base year is projected, not actual
detail: The 30 June 2011 row is a scenario value, not an outturn, so it is not a valid calibration point. Its 1,160 gap against the bulletin is the largest in the calibration table and should be excluded.

item: Projection scope vs bulletin scope
detail: Editions that publish their own base-year actual match the weekly bulletin TOTAL (which includes HMPPS-operated IRCs pre-2022) more closely than the prisons-only figure: mean absolute gap 258 against pop_total versus 394 against pop_prisons. Scoring therefore uses pop_total.

item: Editions publish an unrounded base actual by component
detail: Table 1.1 first row is outturn, not a projection, and is broken down by custody type. Nine such observations exist (Jun 2017, Jun 2018, Jun 2019, Sep 2020, Jul 2021, Nov 2022, Nov 2023, Sep 2024, Sep 2025). This is the only published source of actual population by custody type that sits inside the projection files themselves.

item: Fine defaulters column renamed
detail: Older editions label the column Fine; from the 2020-2026 edition it is Fine Defaulters. Merged to one field.

item: Component matching tolerance
detail: Projection reference days vary between the 1st and last of the month (for example 1 June 2017 against 30 June 2017). Decomposition matches on year and month and records the day gap; the largest gap used is 29 days.

item: No custody-type split
detail: The monthly bulletin is a by-establishment table of Baseline CNA, In Use CNA, Operational Capacity and Population. It carries no remand/sentenced breakdown, so it cannot supply actual components. It is the right source for WP4 supply modelling instead.

item: Capacity is contracting, not flat
detail: Useable operational capacity has fallen from 89,369 on 8 June 2026 to 88,937 on 24 August, about -48 a week on the 13 and 26 week trends. Headroom is being squeezed from both ends: roughly +143/week population and -48/week capacity, so about -190/week combined. Press framing of "97% capacity" hides a shrinking denominator.

item: Bank holiday skip confirmed prospectively
detail: No bulletin published for 31 August 2026 (summer bank holiday). 24 August remains the latest observation, so press figures quoted on 1-2 September derive from the 24 August bulletin.
evidence: gov.uk 2026 weekly page, 31 attachments, refreshed 3 Sep 2026

item: Press headroom figure does not match the bulletin
detail: Reports of "about 1,500 free spaces in the male estate" against an adult male headroom of 1,665 on 24 August. Population as a share of useable operational capacity is 97.6%, consistent with the "97% capacity" claim; as a share of full operational capacity including the 1,640 margin it is 95.9%.
evidence: weekly bulletin 24 Aug 2026 vs BBC/PA reporting

item: Progression release schedule is now a dated input
detail: Revised plan signed into law: 700 on 1 Oct, 650 on 13 Oct, 650 on 10 Nov, 550 on 8 Dec, 600 on 12 Jan 2027, 500 on 9 Feb, 200 on 9 Mar, 200 on 13 Apr. Listed tranches total 4,050 against an estimated 4,500 overall, so residual tranches are undated. Start delayed one month from 2 September; exclusions cut about 1,400 from the original total.

item: 18-year-olds in YOIs is a reclassification, not a release
detail: Holding 18-year-olds in YOIs until shortly before their 19th birthday moves stock from the adult male estate to YCS. It does not reduce the total population but shifts headroom between sub-estates that carry separate operating margins (adult male 1,460, YCS 60). Must be modelled as a transfer or it will look like a spurious release.

item: Monthly panel reconciles exactly to the weekly series
detail: Sum of establishment operational capacity less the operating margin equals the Total row useable operational capacity and the weekly bulletin UOC on the report date. Across 101 months mean absolute UOC gap is 0.5 and mean absolute population gap is 7. This is a hard cross-validation of both parsers.

item: Full operating margin history derived from monthly Total row
detail: Margin = sum of establishment op cap minus the published Total UOC. Path: 2,000 (2018) to 3,000 (May 2020, COVID single-cell working) to 2,750 (Dec 2021), 2,500 (Apr 2022), 2,250 (Jul 2022), 2,000 (Sep 2022), 1,950 (Mar 2023), 1,830 (Apr 2023), 1,680 (Jun 2023), 1,480 (Jul 2023), 1,340 (Sep 2023), 1,350 (Nov 2023), 1,640 (Jul 2025). Thirteen values, more complete than the weekly-derived log.

item: Total row op cap column is UOC, not a sum
detail: The Total row reports useable operational capacity (post-margin), not the sum of the column above it. Summing the column and reading the Total row give different things by exactly the operating margin.
evidence: 2018-03 bulletin, Total row 86,515 vs column sum 88,515

item: Two rows that break naive parsers
detail: Sub total and Total rows sit inside the establishment table and double the estate if counted. Closed or mothballed establishments (Blantyre House 2018-19) publish a partial row with baseline CNA only. The IRC section heading is long enough to trip a footnote length rule and truncate the table.

item: Capacity decline is de-crowding, not cells out of use
detail: Operational capacity fell 900 while baseline CNA fell 32 and in-use CNA fell 116. The estate is operating less crowding above CNA, not losing accommodation. Cells out of use has been roughly flat near 4,000 since 2025.

item: New prison capacity is more than offset by attrition
detail: Millsike added 614 and Fosse Way 227 over twelve months, yet estate operational capacity fell 478 net. In 2026/27 to date new prisons contributed +126 against -1,026 from the rest of the estate. Gross additions are not net additions and the supply model must forecast attrition explicitly.

item: Millsike ramp-up and shortfall
detail: Millsike reached 50% of its eventual peak in 4 months and 90% in 12, faster than Five Wells (8 and 20) or Fosse Way (5 and 31). But it is operating at 1,158 against its own certified 1,468, i.e. 79%, fifteen months after opening, where the older new-builds all sit at 97 to 101% of CNA. Announced capacity has arrived early but short.

item: Establishment-level officer staffing exists and is usable
detail: HMPPS workforce quarterly, annex "Prison and Probation Officer staffing levels against targets", Table 4, gives prison officer staff in post (FTE), target and gap by establishment at eight quarterly dates. 109 establishments, matching 104 of the 122 in the capacity panel on normalised names.

item: Officer staffing against target has deteriorated sharply
detail: Prison officers fell from 69,173 FTE (Mar 2024) to 64,730 (Jun 2026), a loss of 4,443, while targets rose from 68,540 to 70,268. Staffing moved from 101% of target to 92%, and the shortfall from +633 to -5,538 FTE.

item: NEGATIVE RESULT: staffing does not explain which prisons cut capacity
detail: Cross-sectional regression of the change in operational capacity on the change in officer FTE gives slope +0.04 places per FTE, t=0.27, R2=0.001. A placebo window (Mar 2025 to Mar 2026) is also null. The full-span correlation (r=+0.50) is a scale effect, not a crowding effect: in-use CNA correlates with staffing just as strongly (r=+0.52), so the long-run relationship is simply that larger and growing establishments have more officers and more of everything.

item: No establishment-level covariate explains the capacity cuts
detail: Starting crowding level, crowding ratio, staffing as a percentage of target, staffing gap and officer change all give R2 of 0.001. Only establishment size shows anything (r=-0.21) and it is weak. The 29 establishments that cut capacity did start more crowded (103 places above in-use CNA against 57) but the relationship does not hold continuously. This points to central rather than local decision-making.

item: Earlier staffing totals were triple counted
detail: Annex Table 4 contains three aggregate rows inside the establishment column ("All establishments", "Prison Service and YCS Establishment Total", "HMPPS HQ and Area Services Total"). Counting them as establishments tripled the estate total. Corrected band 3-5 officers: 22,802 FTE Mar 2024 to 21,277 Jun 2026, a fall of 1,526 (6.7%), not the 4,443 previously stated. The percentage-of-target figures were unaffected because numerator and denominator were inflated equally.
evidence: src/staffing_test.py; parse_table4 now excludes aggregate rows

item: Annex staffing is not comparable with the main bulletin
detail: Note 44: privately managed prisons are excluded entirely. Note 41: staff in post is hours-adjusted to a 39-hour week to match target staffing, whereas officers work 37, 39 and 41 hour contracts and the main bulletin counts differently. Note 46 warns of job-mapping differences between annex and main publication. Note 50: annex covers band 3-5, not band 3-4.

item: Use the time series file for staffing over time
detail: "Time series of HMPPS staff in post receiving pay on staff in post date" is a 97,451-row panel by date, business group, prison category, establishment and grade, back to March 2017, on a consistent basis. Quarterly tables are not restated (note 16) so cross-release comparisons of the annex are unsafe; this file exists precisely to avoid that.

item: Dartmoor closure from radon
detail: Note 56: Dartmoor staff in post is low because of ongoing radon exposure management, which has led to closure of the prison, redeployment of staff and transfer of prisoners. A named capacity loss with a stated non-financial cause.

item: Hollesley Bay and Warren Hill merged
detail: Note 57: merged into a single prison called Hollesley on the HR system from June 2026. Affects establishment matching between staffing and capacity panels.

item: Deployed resource exceeds staff in post
detail: Notes 53 and 54: Payment Plus (overtime) and detached duty are routinely used to supplement establishments below target and are NOT reflected in staff in post. Note 55: target staffing is the level for an optimal regime, above the minimum needed to operate safely. Note 45: targets cannot be used to calculate vacancies because of governors freedoms. So a shortfall against target is not the same as an unsafe or unstaffed prison.

item: Prisoners per officer worsened while the population fell
detail: Ratio of public sector prison population to band 3-4 officer FTE moved from 3.42 to 3.59 (+5.0%) between Mar 2024 and Jun 2026, and from a best of 3.37 in Sep 2024 (+6.5%). Decomposition: the falling population pushed the ratio DOWN by 0.143, officer losses pushed it UP by 0.315. Entirely an officer-numbers story.

item: Establishment-level safety data exists and is monthly
detail: Safety in Custody summary tables 8a to 8g (assaults by establishment, 2003 onward) and 9a/9b (self-harm by establishment, 2004 onward) are monthly, 156 establishments, matching 111 in the capacity panel. Finer resolution than the quarterly staffing annex.

item: PARTIAL RESULT: assaults associate with capacity cuts, self-harm does not
detail: Establishments that cut operational capacity had an assault rate of 462 per 1,000 in the prior year against 339 for those that did not, difference +122, t=+2.13. But the continuous relationship is weak: slope -0.014 places per point of assault rate, t=-1.54, R2=0.020, and it does not strengthen when controlling for population and starting crowding (multivariate R2=0.027). Self-harm shows nothing at all (t=+0.31, R2=0.001).

item: Assault/self-harm asymmetry is mechanistically coherent
detail: Assaults are a control and order problem that bears directly on how many prisoners can safely be held above certified accommodation; self-harm is a welfare outcome that does not constrain capacity the same way. The asymmetry supports a de-crowding-for-order reading rather than being an artefact, but the effect size remains too small to forecast from.

item: Estate safety levels
detail: Assaults per 1,000 prisoners rose from 716 (2015) to a peak of 1,167 (2018), fell to 749 during COVID, and were 1,075 in 2025. Self-harm per 1,000 rose from 1,130 (2015) to a peak of 2,718 (2024) and was 2,500 in 2025, more than double the 2015 rate. 2026 data covers Q1 only and must not be read as a full year.

item: Table 10 is a ready-made dated supply event log
detail: Safety in Custody Table 10 lists 81 dated prison openings, closings and major re-roles from 1997, including Five Wells (Mar 2022), Fosse Way (May 2023), Millsike (Apr 2025), Cookham Wood YOI to adult (Aug 2024), Lowdham Grange private to public (Aug 2024) and Dartmoor temporarily closed (Sep 2024). This is the dated capacity schedule WP4 needs, already maintained by MoJ.

item: Dartmoor: 689 places withdrawn and still absent
detail: Operational capacity ran down from 689 (Oct 2023) to zero by Aug 2024 over roughly nine months, and has stayed at zero through Jul 2026 while baseline CNA remains recorded at 640. Cause is radon exposure management (workforce annex note 56). It is NOT part of the Mar to Jul 2026 decline, which is separate, but it is 689 places of stranded certified accommodation and a live candidate for reactivation in any supply forecast.

item: RESOLVED: the capacity decline is forecast, and it is maintenance
detail: The Annual Statement on Prison Capacity 2025 (published Jan 2026) projects adult estate supply FALLING from 89,900 in May 2026 to 89,300 in Nov 2026 and 88,300 in May 2027, before recovering to 89,800 by May 2028. The decline I found is not unexplained or unannounced; it is in the published supply path. Annex B states the method: places are projected offline for maintenance work including fire safety and Long Term High Security Estate security improvements, plus a dilapidation assumption based on historic averages.
evidence: MoJ Annual Statement on Prison Capacity 2025, Figure 4 and Annex B

item: MoJ supply projection is scoreable and currently running high
detail: Forecast adult supply for May 2026 was 89,900 against an actual adult useable operational capacity of 89,090, an overshoot of +810. The demand side overshot far more: forecast 88,800 against an actual adult population of 85,647, +3,153. Both errors are in the same direction as the long-run projection bias.

item: Adult-estate UOC is only separable from Oct 2024
detail: The adult estate figure (adult male plus female, excluding YCS) can only be built from the layout B weekly bulletins, so scoring MoJ supply projections against outturn is limited to Oct 2024 onward. Validation: the statement quotes 88,931 useable operational capacity at 29 Sep 2025 and the weekly series gives exactly 88,931, with adult population 87,021 matching too.
evidence: weekly bulletin 29 Sep 2025 vs Annual Statement para 14

item: Crowding is explicitly a managed, reversible lever
detail: HMPPS Annual Report: crowding is "a measure in place to hold two prisoners in a cell designed for one... never desirable and only implemented when deemed safe to do. We continually monitor and take places online and offline depending on prison safety, stability, staffing levels and maintenance needs." So operated crowding is a deliberate dial, which is why no single establishment-level covariate predicts it.

item: Announced additions exclude losses, by MoJ admission
detail: HMPPS Annual Report states its new-places figures "represent only additions to the prison supply and do not account for loss of places during this time (for example due to prison closures or dilapidations)". This confirms the gross-versus-net finding: the 2,900 places delivered since July 2024 is a gross number.

item: Corrected staffing figures validated against MoJ
detail: Annual Statement para 25: staffing at 95% of national target for Band 3-5 prison officers at 30 Sep 2025, a decrease of 1,015 FTE (4.3%) since Sep 2024. My corrected series gives 94.8% at the same date. The earlier triple-counted version could not have been checked this way.

item: Capacity is endogenous to population, and strongly so
detail: Estimated on 13-week changes: d_cap = +670 -0.305*headroom(t-26) +0.420*d_pop, both t-stats above 15, R2=0.463, n=697. Roughly 42% of any population movement is matched by capacity moving the same way. Implied equilibrium headroom with population flat is about 2,200, close to where headroom sits now.

item: The feedback is not a mechanical artefact
detail: Regressing d_cap on headroom(t-13) shares a capacity term across both sides and manufactures negative correlation. Three clean checks survive: d_cap on d_pop alone (+0.416, t=16.7); d_cap on d_pop LAGGED a further 13 weeks, so the population move precedes the capacity move (+0.338, t=12.8); and headroom lagged 26 weeks, putting a full 13-week gap between the capacity terms (-0.300, t=-11.9). The adopted specification uses the 26-week lag plus d_pop.

item: The feedback strengthened sharply in the crisis era
detail: Coefficient on d_pop rises from +0.212 (R2 0.061) in 2011-2019 to +0.567 (R2 0.684) in 2020-2026. Capacity used to move for its own reasons; it is now actively managed against population. Any model fitted on the full sample understates the current strength of the feedback.

item: Endogeneity roughly halves the apparent severity of the outlook
detail: The exogenous-capacity projection had central headroom negative by April 2027; the endogenous version keeps it near 2,000 through winter and reaches the 557 trigger level in June 2027. The difference is entirely the capacity response: capacity is brought back online as headroom tightens. This is a behavioural relationship, not a physical one, and it holds only while there are offline places available to reactivate.

item: Forecast register opened for out-of-sample scoring
detail: Central-case headroom forecasts recorded for seven target dates from 25 Sep 2026 to 28 May 2027, to be scored against the weekly bulletins as they publish. First scoreable point is the bulletin for 28 September 2026.

item: asfreq(7D) silently destroys the post-Oct-2024 series
detail: The weekly grid must not be built with asfreq. The grid anchors on the first observation (Friday 7 Jan 2011) but the reporting day moved to Monday on 21 Oct 2024, so no later observation lands on the grid; asfreq returns NaN throughout and any fill produces a flat line. The previous capacity-feedback estimate lost the last 94 weeks (n=697 against 791). src/weekly_grid.py builds the grid from the observation sequence instead and inserts the 30 genuinely skipped weeks.

item: Corrected capacity feedback coefficients
detail: Full sample: d_cap = +627 -0.284*headroom(t-26) +0.386*d_pop, t = -14.4 and +19.4, R2=0.418, n=791. Crisis era 2020+: -0.174 (t=-4.5), +0.474 (t=+21.3), R2=0.575. Clean precedence check d_cap ~ d_pop(t-13): +0.316, t=+13.4. Equilibrium headroom 2,203, absorption 39%. Close to the buggy estimates because pre-2024 data dominated, but the crisis-era terms moved most.

item: The population trend has no stable sign
detail: OLS slope by window: 8wk +7,421/yr; 13wk +4,443; 26wk -2,018; 52wk -1,701; 104wk -181; 156wk -357; 260wk +1,710; 520wk +366; full 817wk -65/yr. The sign flips four times. Any single trend estimate is an artefact of the window chosen, and a long-horizon projection built on one is not a forecast.

item: Trend extrapolation is actively harmful at long horizons
detail: Walk-forward on the full series, population MAE: naive no-change 2,052 (1yr), 3,560 (2yr), 4,794 (3yr), 5,541 (5yr), 2,646 (7yr), 1,191 (10yr). Drift on a 52-week trend: 2,887 / 5,219 / 6,948 / 12,088 / 9,538 / 4,952. Drift on a 260-week trend: 2,384 / 4,226 / 5,824 / 7,628 / 4,480 / 1,416. Naive beats BOTH drift specifications at every horizon from one to ten years. At five years the 52-week drift error is more than double naive.

item: Forecast error dwarfs the headroom buffer
detail: Naive MAE at five years is 5,541 people (6.6%). Current headroom is 2,094. So the irreducible five-year forecast error is nearly three times the entire operating buffer. Ten-year statements about headroom are not meaningfully constrained by evidence.

item: PAC: net capacity gain of 1,005 places in fourteen years
detail: Public Accounts Committee: between May 2010 and September 2024 HMPPS added a net 1,005 places (new places minus places lost) against 6,518 gross delivered, so attrition absorbed 85% of gross additions. A written answer gives operational capacity rising from 89,757 (May 2010) to 90,212 (Jul 2024), +455. My series independently gives 89,936 (Jan 2011) to 90,212 (Jul 2024), +276, and 90,577 now: +641 net over 15.6 years. Three sources agree the net figure is a few hundred places.

item: What the minister s ten years rests on
detail: The 10-Year Prison Capacity Strategy (Dec 2024) commits to 14,000 places by 2031 at up to GBP 7bn, with a demand assumption of +3,000 prisoners a year. Realised population growth 2011 to 2026 is +246/yr. If the historical net-to-gross ratio holds, 14,000 gross implies about 2,150 net. The Annual Statement itself labels its post-2030 extrapolation experimental and illustrative only, holding court capacity and sentencing practice constant at March 2030 levels.
evidence: 10-Year Prison Capacity Strategy; Annual Statement 2025 Annex A

item: Sustained +3,000/yr has never happened over five years
detail: Rolling windows on the weekly series: 11% of 2-year and 6% of 3-year windows reach +3,000/yr or more, so fast growth does occur. But 0% of 5-year windows reach even +2,000/yr. The fastest 5-year run on record is +1,968/yr, and that is the COVID rebound off an artificially depressed base. Median growth is NEGATIVE at every window length: -248/yr over 2 years, -96 over 3, -220 over 5.

item: The flat 15-year average is not a COVID artefact
detail: Pre-COVID, Jan 2011 to Feb 2020, 9.1 years: +96/yr (82,991 to 83,868). Essentially flat for a decade before COVID. COVID fall -5,392/yr over 1.1 years. Post-COVID recovery +2,472/yr over 3.5 years. SDS40 era +454/yr. So the flat long-run average is a genuinely flat pre-COVID decade plus a fall and rebound, not an averaging illusion.

item: +3,000/yr is the near-term counterfactual, not a central forecast
detail: In both the Dec 2024 strategy and the Jan 2026 Annual Statement the figure is prefixed "without further action". It reconciles with Figure 5 over the first two years (+2,900/yr) but the counterfactual itself decelerates to +1,850/yr in years 3-4 and +1,300/yr in years 5-6. The CENTRAL path including the Sentencing Act is +900/yr over two years and +1,333/yr over six. Quoting +3,000/yr as a ten-year central expectation misstates MoJ on both counts.

item: The projections are conditional, which is why they overshoot
detail: MoJ projects the population under existing release rules; the rules then change in response; the projection overshoots. The WP2 decomposition supports this: 95% of projection error sits in the determinate sentenced population, which is precisely the component set by release policy. A large part of the measured overshoot is therefore the size of the policy response, not forecast incompetence. This does not rescue the projections as a planning basis, because a counterfactual systematically falsified by the publisher own subsequent actions cannot anchor a GBP 7bn build programme.

item: SENTENCE INFLATION: 21% more custodial time on 1.5% fewer sentences
detail: All-offence average custodial sentence length rose from 16.3 to 20.1 months (+23.3%) while the number of immediate custodial sentences fell from 90,500 to 89,164 (-1.5%). Total custodial months issued per year rose from 1.48m to 1.79m, +21.5%. Under an unchanged release fraction that implies a sentenced population about 21% higher. The actual total population rose 1.5%.

item: The mix shifted from short to long, not just the average
detail: Sentences under 6 months fell from 46,855 (51.8% of all custodial sentences) to 40,136 (45.0%), -14.3%. Sentences over 4 years rose from 7,328 (8.1%) to 9,163 (10.3%), +25.0%. Over 15 years and less than life rose 141%, over 10 years +49%, over 3 to 4 years +46%. Life sentences fell 48%. The distribution is being stretched at the top and hollowed at the bottom.

item: Sentence inflation is concentrated in specific offence groups
detail: Average custodial sentence length by group: miscellaneous crimes against society +33.9% (10.9 to 14.6 months), public order +27.9% (6.8 to 8.7), fraud +22.8% (18.0 to 22.1), sexual offences +20.8% (61.2 to 73.9). Theft went the OTHER way, -14.3% (9.1 to 7.8), as did all summary offences. So it is not general inflation; it is a widening gap between serious and volume crime.

item: Charging and prosecution volumes fell while custody held flat
detail: Defendants proceeded against fell from 1,493,801 to 1,360,615 (-8.9%). Cautions fell from 119,724 to 40,195 (-66%). Other out of court resolutions fell 99%, from 72,441 to 882. Community resolutions rose 57%. Summary custodial sentences fell 38.9%, summary non-motoring -46.6%. Indictable custodial sentences rose 6.6%. The funnel narrowed at the top and lengthened at the bottom.

item: The flat population is two large forces cancelling
detail: Sentence inflation implies roughly +21% on the sentenced stock over a decade. Release-point cuts run the other way: 50% to 40% (SDS40, Sep 2024) to one third (progression, Oct 2026), a factor of about 1.5 on time actually served. The apparently boring flat population line is the net of a large upward push from sentencing and a large downward push from executive release. This also explains the WP2 finding that 95% of MoJ projection error sits in the determinate component.
evidence: synthesis of CJS and weekly series

item: Sentence inflation is comprehensively covered
detail: Sentencing Academy (Pina-Sanchez, Roberts, Bild, Apr 2025) measures severity as custody rate x ACSL against an ONS Crime Severity Score, 2005-2024, all offence groups: severity +62%, crime seriousness +8%, so 87% is genuine inflation and sentencing is 54% more punitive than 2005. Violence and weapons doubled, fraud tripled, drugs and public order show no discernible pattern. Also: Howard League judicial critique (2024, four former Lord Chief Justices), MoJ ACSL analysis 2010-2023 (2025), MoJ Story of the Prison Population 1993-2012, Gauke Independent Sentencing Review Part 1 (2025). Do not present sentence inflation as a finding.
evidence: Measuring Sentence Inflation in England and Wales, Sentencing Academy

item: Their index deliberately excludes volume, so it does not map to places
detail: The Imprisonment Index is custody rate x ACSL: the severity of the AVERAGE case. It contains no volume term, so it cannot be converted into demand for prison places. Their stated future research directions are guilty pleas, previous convictions, statutory minima, magistrates powers, punitive populism and budget cuts. Release fractions, time served, capacity and the prison population are absent throughout. The bridge from sentencing severity to prison places is unoccupied.

item: The flat population is NOT sentence inflation offset by release
detail: Earlier framing was wrong. Bridge Jun 2017 to Sep 2025: custodial months imposed +9.9% (ACSL +19.8%, volume -8.2%), but the DETERMINATE population fell 16.5%, from 57,726 to 48,224, a loss of 9,502. Release cuts more than absorbed sentence inflation. The total population rose 1.9% only because remand grew 83.6% (+8,062) and recall grew 98.1% (+6,267). Sentenced prisoners were replaced by unsentenced and recalled ones, close to one for one.

item: Composition shift is real, not definitional, and COVID-initiated
detail: Determinate share of the population fell from 67.2% to 55.1% while remand plus recall rose from 18.7% to 34.7%. The break is Jun 2019 to Sep 2020: determinate -8,103, remand +3,246, recall +1,858, when courts stopped. Recall then rises steadily every period with no step, so it is not a reclassification. The shift never reversed.

item: This explains the WP2 error decomposition exactly
detail: MoJ projected determinate to grow on sentence inflation; release policy cut it instead (determinate error +8,610 in 2020-onward editions). MoJ missed the remand surge (remand error -2,862). The two errors offset, which is why gross projection error is 1.9x net. The composition finding and the decomposition finding are the same phenomenon seen from two directions.

item: Recall volume nearly doubled in three years
detail: Recalls per quarter: 6,824 (Q1 2023), 7,415 (Q1 2024), 10,101 (Q1 2025), 14,349 (Q4 2025), 13,193 (Q1 2026). Annualised 27,820 to 51,419, +85%. The inflection sits between Q1 2024 and Q1 2025, which brackets SDS40 in September 2024. 99.4% of recalls result in return to custody.

item: KEY FINDING: the recall loop was contained by shortening recalls, not reducing them
detail: Recall inflow rose 73% (29,660 to 51,419 a year) while the recall STOCK rose 0.6% (12,579 to 12,657). The reconciliation is duration: implied mean time in custody per recall fell from 5.09 to 2.95 months, -42%. Achieved by shifting to fixed-term recalls, which are now 72% of all recalls (14-day 34.9%, 28-day 35.6%, 56-day 1.3%) against 27% standard determinate.
evidence: recall stock from projection actuals; inflow from OMSQ Table 5.Q.1; composition Table 5.Q.13

item: The containment is fragile and threatens the headroom forecast
detail: Recall stock = inflow x duration. Duration has already been cut 42% and 72% of recalls are already fixed-term, so there is limited room to cut further. If the progression model raises licence population and inflow by 35% with duration held, recall stock rises about 4,430, which is close to the entire 4,500 of the release programme and more than twice current headroom of 2,094. Only if duration falls a further 15% does the increase stay under 2,000.

item: The standing forecast has no recall feedback
detail: headroom_model_v2 treats the release tranches as pure one-off stock reductions. It contains no term for released prisoners returning on recall. Given the loop measured above, this is the most likely way the forecast fails, and the failure would be a systematic OPTIMISTIC bias appearing roughly one to two quarters after each tranche.

item: MAJOR: 56-day fixed-term recall replaced the 14 and 28 day recalls
detail: OMSQ recall note 12: from 31 March 2026 a 56-day Fixed-Term Recall replaced the previous 14-day and 28-day fixed-term recalls for eligible offenders. This runs OPPOSITE to the duration-shortening that had been containing the recall population. On Q1 2026 volumes (4,599 at 14 days, 4,699 at 28 days) fixed-term recall days per quarter go from 195,958 to 520,688, a factor of 2.66, implying the fixed-term recall population rises from about 2,153 to 5,722, roughly +3,570 places. Current headroom is 2,094.
evidence: OMSQ licence-recall Jan-Mar 2026, Notes sheet note 12

item: The summer population rise is probably FTR56, not seasonality or demand
detail: Population bottomed at 85,704 on 27 April 2026 and has risen steadily since, reaching 86,843 by 24 August (+1,139). The 56-day recall took effect 31 March, so the stock would build over roughly two months and show through from June. The +143/week trend used in the headroom projection is therefore a policy transition bedding in, not a trend to extrapolate. It should level off once the new recall stock reaches equilibrium.

item: Recall composition series has a break; totals do not
detail: Recall note 11: fixed-term and standard determinate recall figures before July 2025 are not comparable with later figures, because some recalls were previously recorded as emergency without a fixed-term or standard designation and sat in an Other category. So the rise in the fixed-term SHARE is partly reclassification and the "72% fixed-term" figure must not be compared with earlier periods. The total recall counts in Tables 5.Q.1 and 5.Q.2 are unaffected, so the near-doubling of recall volume stands.

item: Recall intensity per release rose 56%, and recalls now exceed releases
detail: Recalls per 1,000 determinate releases in the same quarter: 565 mean across 2023 to Q1 2024, 882 mean across 2025 to Q1 2026, reaching 1,017 in Q1 2026. Releases rose only 12% while recalls rose 75%, so this is an intensity effect not a volume artefact. In Q1 2026 there were 13,193 recalls against 12,977 determinate releases: more people returned on recall than were released from determinate sentences.

item: Two corrections to the standing forecast, in opposite directions
detail: First, the +143/week population slope is a transitional FTR56 effect and should decay, which makes the near-term outlook better than forecast. Second, the model has no recall feedback, and the FTR56 change alone implies up to +3,570 places still to arrive, which makes it worse. Net direction unclear until the FTR56 equilibrium is estimated. The forecast register lodged for 25 Sep 2026 onward should be treated as superseded pending that work.

item: MAJOR CORRECTION: the population has a strong annual cycle and I was extrapolating it
detail: Week-of-year deviation from a 53-week centred mean, amplitude 859 people: trough week 1 (January, -407 by month), peak week 44 (November, +365). Monthly: Jan -407, Jun -257, Jul -55, Aug +183, Oct +340, Nov +365, Dec +13. The +143/week slope used in v1 and v2 was fitted over Apr-Aug, the fastest-rising part of the cycle, and extrapolated forward from late August, just before the peak. Roughly half the observed summer rise was seasonal.

item: Deseasonalised underlying trend is +19/week, not +143
detail: Observed rise 20 Apr to 24 Aug 2026 was +770. Expected seasonal rise over the same weeks is +411. Residual +359 over 18 weeks = +19.1/week once deseasonalised. Fitted on only 19 weeks, so fragile, and it absorbs whatever the FTR56 change is contributing.

item: FTR56 hypothesis NOT supported by the shape of the rise
detail: A 56-day recall stock building from 31 March would saturate over about 8 weeks. The observed path is flat from late April to end June and then rises linearly from early July, 14 weeks after the change. A saturating curve fit fails to identify (tau diverges, degenerating to linear). So FTR56 may be contributing but it cannot be the main driver of the summer rise on timing grounds. The Apr-Jun 2026 OMSQ, due about 29 October, is the first release that can measure it directly.

item: Seasonal correction reverses the outlook, and the trend is now the dominant uncertainty
detail: Central case (trend +19/wk, tranches as announced): headroom never enters the historical trigger band and rises to about 4,000 through 2027. But sensitivity is extreme: at +40/wk the band is entered Nov 2027, at +60/wk Sep 2027, at +100/wk Jun 2027, at +143/wk Sep 2026. The whole forecast now rests on a trend estimated from 19 weeks.

item: Scoring the "bust before Christmas" claim under v3
detail: With no releases and the fitted +19/wk trend, headroom at Christmas 2026 is 2,269 and never falls below 557. The claim requires an underlying trend of about +150/week to leave headroom near 557 by Christmas, and +200/week to exhaust it. That is 8 to 10 times the deseasonalised rate observed since April. Under v1 assumptions (+143/wk) the claim held; under v3 it does not. The earlier validation of the ministerial claim is withdrawn.

item: CORRECTION: the recall surge began with ECSL, not SDS40
detail: Filling the Oct-Dec 2024 edition gives the full quarterly series. Recalls jumped from 7,415 (Q1 2024) to 9,782 (Q2 2024), +32% in one quarter, then 9,975 and 10,401. SDS40 was September 2024, so the inflection precedes it. It coincides with ECSL extension to 60 days (March 2024) and 70 days (May 2024) and Operation Early Dawn (May 2024). Earlier attribution to SDS40 is withdrawn.

item: Long-run: recalls per 100 releases rose from 29 to 66, and to about 85 in 2025
detail: Annual series from OMSQ 2024 annual tables. Releases from custody fell 23% (74,443 to 57,277) while recalls rose 75% (21,467 to 37,573), then 48,327 in 2025 (+125% on 2015). The ratio of recalls to releases more than doubled. Fewer people leave, and a rising share of those who do come back.

item: Long-run sentence length and time served, with a 2024 artefact
detail: Mean sentence of those released: 18.4 to 25.2 months by 2023 (+37%), with 2024 at 30.0 inflated by the SDS40 cohort released that autumn. Time served 11.2 to 15.2 by 2023 (+36%). Proportion served held at 60 to 64% every year 2015 to 2023, then 55.5% in 2024. Nine years of stability then a five-point drop confirms the quarterly picture.

item: What sustainable footing has ever looked like: 10 weeks in 15 years
detail: In 817 weeks headroom exceeded 5,000 in 10 weeks, the last in February 2013, and never exceeded 7,000. It exceeded 3,000 in 16.5% of weeks and 2,000 in 56.8%. Longest unbroken run above 2,000: 77 weeks, ending September 2013. Occupancy has averaged 96 to 99% in every calendar year; it was under 95% in 25 weeks, the last in April 2020. The MoJ 2032 destination (supply 98,900, demand 95,900, headroom 3,000) is a level seen in one week in six since 2011.

item: 2026 is the best year for headroom since 2013
detail: Mean headroom Jan to Aug 2026 is 2,927 with a minimum of 2,094, against 1,130 (min 557) in 2023, 1,831 in 2024 and 1,838 in 2025. The year the government describes as perma-crisis has had more headroom than any year since 2013. The Sentencing Act commencement in March did what it was meant to.

item: Early editions had no like-for-like benchmark; now sourced
detail: The 2008, 2009 and 2010 editions base years predate the weekly series, so the no-change benchmark was NaN for 16 of 75 targets and those rows were silently counted as naive losses and as wrong-direction calls. Base populations are now taken from the Population in Custody bulletins: 30 June 2008 83,194 (June 2009 bulletin, year-ago column), 30 June 2009 83,391 (June 2010 bulletin, revised), 30 June 2010 85,002. All 75 targets now have a benchmark computed on identical targets.

item: Direction accuracy is 63%, not 43%
detail: The 43% figure in the first draft was depressed by the 16 targets with a NaN base, which returned sign(NaN) and were scored as wrong. Corrected: 63% overall, 53% at one and two years; projections called a rise in 73% of targets against 52% actual. "Barely better than a coin toss at short horizons and biased toward growth" replaces "worse than a coin toss".

item: Table 1 and Table 2 were not like-for-like in the first draft
detail: Naive MAE was averaged over targets with a benchmark while MoJ MAE covered all targets. Recomputed on identical targets: naive MAE by horizon 1,666 / 2,275 / 3,222 / 3,595 / 2,630 / 2,439 against MoJ 2,429 / 3,923 / 3,616 / 5,115 / 4,778 / 3,780. Naive closer on 54 of 75 targets. Conclusion unchanged; numbers moved.

item: Table 3 row for 2008-2015 was misaligned by one column
detail: Values were transcribed from a fixed-width print where blank cells collapsed. The 2008 edition has no scoreable 1 or 2 year target (2009 and 2010 predate the series); its 3, 4 and 5 year errors are +3.0, +2.7, +5.7. The table is now generated programmatically and out-of-range cells are marked n/a.

item: The no-change forecast wins in the pre-emergency-release era on identical targets
detail: 2008 to 2014 editions: naive MAE 1,623 against MoJ 2,895, naive closer on 29 of 40 targets. These editions predate ECSL (2023), SDS40 (2024) and the progression model (2026). The conditional-projection defence cannot explain an overshoot that existed a decade before the policy responses it cites.

item: Headline survives every cut; magnitude does not
detail: Excluding COVID targets: +3.2%, 82% too high, naive closer 72%. Excluding release-scheme targets: +3.2%, 82%, 71%. Excluding both (normal years, n=56): +2.3%, 79%, 71%. Pre-2020 editions on normal years: +2.1%, 77%, 73%. Prisons-only outturn: +3.9%, 84%, 74%. Dropping five largest errors: +3.2%, 83%, 70%. Naive wins at every horizon under every cut. About 40% of the measured overshoot is the two shock periods; the structural overshoot is about +2%.

item: Edition-level inference
detail: 15/17 editions mean error > 0, sign test p=0.0012. 13/17 naive MAE < MoJ MAE, p=0.0245. Mean of edition means +4.23%, sd 3.62, t=4.81 on n=17. Editions share target years so even 17 overstates independence.

item: Two objections the data cannot settle
detail: (1) Regime dependence: the naive benchmark wins because the population was flat; it would have lost 1993-2012 when the MoJ method was built. (2) Capacity binding through non-release channels (remand, HDC, sentencing) could make pre-2020 overshoot constrained demand rather than error. Proportion served stable at 60-64% through 2015-2023 argues against a binding release constraint but does not rule out other channels.

item: THIRD ACT: remand has turned, down 14% from its peak
detail: Monthly remand population (OMSQ Table 1.A.1) peaked at 17,947 in August 2025 and fell to 15,386 by June 2026, -2,561 (-14.3%). It fell in nine of the ten months. The Crown Court backlog has not cleared (trial dates being set for late 2028), so this is judicial discretion: courts bailing defendants they would previously have remanded because a two-year wait in custody untried is judged unfair. The PAC recommended in March 2025 that remand be brought back to 2019 levels (about 9,150), which it said would free 8,000 places; about a third of that has now happened.

item: The H1 2026 population fall was substantially remand, not the Sentencing Act
detail: I attributed the spring 2026 fall to the Sentencing Act commencement. The monthly split shows April 2026: remand -663, sentenced -968, so both. But from December 2025 to June 2026 the sentenced population ROSE 1,404 while remand fell 1,242. The sustained decline is unconvicted prisoners leaving on bail, not sentenced prisoners leaving early. The earlier line that 2026 headroom shows the Act "did what it was meant to" is withdrawn as an attribution; the headroom figures themselves stand.

item: A fourth policy-like lever in the headroom equation
detail: Headroom is now being moved by four discretionary levers, none of them demand: release tranches (down), FTR56 (up), planned maintenance (capacity down), and bail decisions (remand down, about -200 a month since August 2025). The bail lever is contested in real time: the Met Commissioner is warning that courts are failing to remand dangerous suspects. If that pressure succeeds, remand rises again. The headroom model contains none of this and should be read as a baseline that four policy switches sit on top of.

item: The scorecard remand finding is about to invert
detail: The 2020-onward editions under-projected remand by 2,862 on average. Remand is now falling at a pace that, if sustained, would make the 2025-2030 edition remand assumption too HIGH within its first year. The two offsetting errors (determinate high, remand low) that made gross error 1.9x net could become two errors in the same direction.

item: MoJ itself says remand data is weak
detail: HMCTS told the PAC that MoJ data relating to the remand population are not accurate enough for MoJ to draw insights from. The monthly series here is the published one and reconciles to the weekly totals, but time-on-remand and custody-time-limit breach data are acknowledged by MoJ to be unreliable. One in twenty remand prisoners had been held over two years (PAC, March 2025).

item: The remand fall is a transfer from one queue to another, not a resolution
detail: Crown Court open for-trial cases rose from 64,388 to 67,419 (+3,031). Defendants in custody fell 1,124 (17,409 to 16,285; share 27% to 24%). Defendants on bail rose 4,098 (46,177 to 50,275). Bailed open cases are now 2.61x the Q4 2019 level and the mean time a bailed case has been open is 353 days, 2.12x 2019. The prison remand population fell because cases moved from the custody queue to the bail queue, which is longer and slower.

item: STORED CUSTODY: the bail shift defers custody to 2027-28, it does not remove it
detail: A remanded defendant has time on remand credited against sentence; many are released at sentencing having already served. A bailed defendant convicted in 2028 serves the full custodial portion from sentencing. For the 4,098 extra bailed open cases since Q2 2025, at 80% conviction, 50% custody rate, 22.3 month mean sentence and 40% served, about 14,600 prisoner-months (1,200 prisoner-years) of custody is deferred to when the trials happen. Range 700 to 1,800 prisoner-years on plausible assumptions. Offsets: acquittals avoid custody entirely, and case attrition over long delays reduces convictions. The counterfactual is the same custody earlier, so this is timing, but timing concentrated into the years the building programme is meant to relieve.
evidence: assumptions stated; CJS Q5_2b custody rates; OMSQ time served

item: Five institutions, no one controlling the total
detail: Ministers set release points (down). HMPPS sets operated crowding, maintenance timing and recall length (both directions). The judiciary sets bail (down since Aug 2025) and sentence length (up, structurally). Police set charging and are now applying pressure on bail (up). Parliament sets sentencing law (up). The population is the net of five hands on five levers, each responding to the others, which is why it is flat and why no projection conditional on any one of them holds.

item: Sentencing dates ARE tracked, by MoJ, quarterly, and they have moved a long way
detail: CCSQ Table T4: mean days from offence to completion at the Crown Court 480 (2019) to 712 (Q1 2026), +48%; pre-court (offence to charge) 327 to 421, at-court 154 to 266. Table C8: mean wait from sending to trial start, defendants on bail 21.7 weeks (2019) to 44.1 (Q1 2026), doubled; defendants in custody 15.7 to 22.9. Table O2: mean time a bailed open case has been waiting 167 to 353 days. Tracked by the Commons Library (CBP-8372), NAO (2024), PAC (2025) and the Leveson review. What is not usually quoted is the split by remand status, and nobody links it to prison composition.
evidence: outputs/crown_court_open_by_remand.csv; CCSQ Tables C8, O2, T4

item: NEW COMPOSITE: people active in a criminal justice process
detail: Prison population + supervision in the community (court orders and post-release licence, from probation caseload) + defendants on bail awaiting Crown Court trial. Pre-release supervision excluded to avoid counting prisoners twice; magistrates open cases excluded (mostly non-custodial and dominated by non-attendance). Dec 2019: 82,868 + 172,110 + 19,261 = 274,239. Mar 2026: 87,342 + 179,300 + 50,275 = 316,917. Up 42,678 (+15.6%) while prison rose 5.4%. Bail accounts for 73% of the increase. Prison is 27.6% of the total. US analogue: BJS "correctional populations" (prison + jail + probation + parole); no E&W equivalent is published.

item: Composite caveats
detail: Probation caseload has a series break at 31 March 2026 (note 49), so part of the +12,000 in community supervision between Mar 2025 and Mar 2026 may be definitional. A person can be on a court order and on licence simultaneously; the community figure is the deduplicated MoJ total. Crown Court bail counts cases not people (a defendant can have more than one case). Magistrates court open cases (about 300,000) are excluded and would roughly double the total if included, but most carry no custody risk.

item: Prison plus probation is an established measure; bail is not
detail: The Council of Europe SPACE I and II statistics compute a "correctional rate" (prison plus probation per 100,000) for every member state; McNeill and Beyens (2013) and McNeill (2018, Pervasive Punishment) built the "mass supervision" literature on it and cite E&W March 2013 prison 83,769 against 224,823 under community supervision. The US BJS publishes prison + jail + probation + parole annually since 1985. NONE of these include people released on bail awaiting trial. That component is the novel addition and it accounts for 73% of the E&W increase since 2019.
evidence: SPACE II; McNeill 2018; BJS Correctional Populations series

item: The prison-plus-probation limb reproduces the SPACE rate
detail: E&W prison plus community supervision per 100,000 population: 416 in 2024 on this construction. McNeill cites Scotland at 548, described as 125% of E&W, implying E&W about 440. Consistent to within the definitional differences. The construction is therefore comparable with the international literature.

item: SHAPE: the US and E&W do not line up
detail: US total correctional population fell 26% from its 2007 peak (7.3m to 5.4m by 2022), driven by community supervision down 23%; the rate fell from 3,210 to 2,060 per 100,000 adults over fifteen consecutive years. E&W prison plus probation was flat: 251,274 (2015) to 252,947 (2024), +0.7%, with a 2017 peak and a Transforming Rehabilitation era decline. E&W justice-held with bail rose from 280,134 (2015) to 316,917 (Mar 2026), +13%. Bail share 7% (2019) to 16% (2026). Composition is similar (incarcerated about a third in both) but direction is opposite. E&W rate 660 per 100,000 adults, 1 in 151; US 2,100, 1 in 48.

item: Is the justice-held population the more interesting finding?
detail: As an organising frame, yes: it explains why the prison line is flat (displacement into buckets the state does not have to build for), unifies the substitution, the bail shift, the recall loop and the scorecard, and has a time series. As a publishable claim it is weaker than the scorecard: the bail limb counts cases not people, the probation series breaks in March 2026, and magistrates open cases are excluded by judgement. Recommended use: the frame of the working paper, with the scorecard as the evidence and the composite as the chart on page one.

item: March 2026 probation break: measured and fixable
detail: Note 49: a new data pipeline captures more cases from Q1 2026 onward, not backcast. Measured as the last quarterly change less the mean of the three prior quarterly changes: all supervision +7,707 (3.1% of level), of which pre-release +4,220 (excluded from the composite), all supervision in the community +3,623 (2.1%), court orders +2,502, post-release +1,263. Old-basis March 2026 community supervision is therefore about 175,677 against 179,300 published. Underlying growth before the break was about +2,181 a quarter, so the community limb was genuinely rising about 5% a year through 2025, consistent with more people on licence after early release.

item: Magistrates custody-risk limb built from Table M1
detail: Open magistrates cases by class. Either-way plus indictable-only "for trial" cases are the custody-risk limb: 47,085 (Q4 2019) to 83,020 (Q1 2026), +76%, now above the COVID peak of 76,163. Summary motoring (185,690, mostly Single Justice Procedure) and summary non-motoring (85,624) excluded as carrying no realistic custody outcome. Breaches (16,388) excluded because those people are already in the probation limb.

item: JUSTICE-HELD POPULATION v2: +23%, and 89% of the increase is people waiting for trial
detail: Prison + community supervision (break-adjusted) + Crown Court bail + magistrates custody-risk cases. Dec 2019: 82,868 + 172,110 + 19,261 + 47,085 = 321,324. Mar 2026: 87,342 + 175,677 + 50,275 + 83,020 = 396,314. Up 74,990 (+23.3%). Of the increase: prison 6%, community 5%, Crown Court bail 41%, magistrates 48%. People awaiting trial with custody risk now number 133,295, 1.5 times the prison population. Prison is 22% of the total. One in 121 adults.

item: Remaining caveats on the composite
detail: (1) Bail and magistrates limbs count cases, not people. (2) A person can sit in two limbs, for example on licence and bailed for a new charge; the overlap is unquantified and would reduce the total. (3) Magistrates for-trial cases include a small number of defendants in custody who are also in the prison limb; custody time limits at magistrates are 56 days so the overlap is small. (4) The M1 series starts in 2019, so v2 has no pre-2019 history; v1 (without magistrates) runs from 2015 and shows the same direction.

item: Time-to-recall distribution is not published
detail: No MoJ table gives recalls by time since release. Nearest proxies: HMI Probation 2018 found 37% of recalls were of people who had served under 12 months, whose licences are short, implying recall within months; HMI Prisons "Recall, release, repeat" (Nov 2025) describes the 14-day cycle qualitatively; HMI Probation recall thematic (2020). MoJ statisticians (Aug 2026) attribute the recall rise to early release putting more on licence and to fixed-term recalls allowing repeat recall of the same person. An FOI for recalls by weeks since release, by release type, would settle it and is the one number that would convert the register warning into a forecast term.

item: SCORECARD: the MoJ assumed the determinate recall rate would stay constant; it doubled
detail: Prison Population Projections 2021-2026, section on recall: "The rate at which offenders from determinate sentences are recalled to prison is assumed to remain constant." Recalls per 100 determinate releases rose from about 47 (2021) to 85 (2025). This is a specific, stated, falsified assumption and belongs in the scorecard note beside the determinate finding: the two components policy moved most were the two the projections held fixed.
evidence: Prison Population Projections 2021 to 2026, p.4; outputs/longrun_releases_recalls.csv

item: Who discusses the underlying shape
detail: Components, yes: MoJ OMSQ bulletins report remand and recall as "record highs" every quarter with attributions (court recovery, longer sentences, more on licence); PRT Bromley Briefings track recalls and caseloads; PAC (2025) pressed on remand; HMI Prisons and Probation on recall practice; McNeill on mass supervision. "Managed to a number", partly: the Owers review (occupancy under 95% once in twelve years) and the Annual Statement describe capacity management explicitly. What nobody does is put the two together: treat the headline as a control variable and the composition as the outcome. Each component is reported as an isolated record; the substitution between them is not.

item: Attribution and the methodology asset
detail: All deliverables now attributed to Walk Forward Research. The justice-held population methodology note v1.0 is written as the citable object: definition, exclusions, construction table, relationship to SPACE/BJS/McNeill, break adjustment, six numbered limitations, planned refinements, CC BY 4.0 licence, suggested citation with DOI placeholder. This is the document that carries priority; the series is credited to whoever wrote its definition and keeps publishing it.
